historical_claims.anchor: Ralph Ellison grew up in Oklahoma City in a family that valued books and music.
His father died when he was young, and his mother supported the household through demanding jobs.
He attended Tuskegee Institute to study music and encountered both the possibilities and constraints of an institution shaped by segregation and ideals of racial advancement.
In 1936 Ellison traveled to New York, intending to earn money that would let him continue his studies.
When Invisible Man won the National Book Award for fiction in 1953, Ellison's first published novel had become a major work of American literature.
The book draws upon American modernist experiment and upon Black vernacular cultural forms that a narrow account of modernism might exclude.
